newsitem.title: USA: UMAX offers new low-price Mac compatibles.
newsitem.headline: UMAX offers new low-price Mac compatibles.

text.p: Umax Computer Corp. said Tuesday it is offering a new entry-level personal computer at the lowest price available for Macintosh-compatible machines -- $1,349 -- and cut prices for all its products by up to 20 percent.

Umax, the Fremont, Calif.-based U.S. subsidiary of Taiwan's Umax Data Systems, is one of a handful of companies making computers that licenses Apple Computer Inc.'s operating system, allowing them to build Macintosh-compatible personal computers, or clones.

UMAX's move to cut prices comes amid concerns about falling market share for Apple's own Macintosh-brand computers over the last year. Analysts consider UMAX's growth to have come largely at the expense of Apple.
In addition to the $1,349 price for its new SuperMac C500/180, Umax is offering a $50 manufacturers' rebate for a limited time. The computer runs on a 180-megahertz PowerPC 603E microprocessor.
The machine is targeted at the consumer and education markets, Umax said.
The SuperMac C500 ships with 16 megabytes of random access memory, a CD-ROM player, a 1.2-gigabyte hard drive, a keyboard and a mouse. A monitor must be purchased separately.
Umax Computer said it was reducing prices immediately for all its SuperMac models, with price cuts ranging from about 7 percent to 20 percent.

For example, its SuperMac C600/200-megahertz machine now carries a street price of $1,799, a savings of $200 from the previous price. The high-end SuperMac S900/200 with a dual-processor system is now $4,499, a $300 reduction.

In another development involving Macintosh clones, Be Inc., a company developing a new computer operating system, was expected to announce with Motorola Inc. that Be's system will be included in Motorola's Macintosh-compatible computers, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
The newspaper, which interviewed Jean-Louis Gassee, the former Apple executive who heads Be, said Be is close to a similar pact with International Business Machines Corp.

Be, based in Menlo Park, Calif., has already announced deals with other Macintosh clone makers. It failed to sell its system to Apple but believes pacts with Motorola and IBM are equal or better than one with Apple because IBM and Motorola are Apple's partners in developing the Macintosh's PowerPC chips, the report said.
